title: Cotten (2021): Professor Question Practice
instructions: Practice a 30-second response: state your conclusion, then connect the life course, specific forms of use, evidence strength, and social or technical conditions. Keep statistics and policy descriptions tied to the chapter's historical context, and label applications as inferences.

cards.title: How does the chapter distinguish ICTs from emerging technologies?
cards.answer_30s: Information and communication technologies, or ICTs, are devices and applications for gathering and exchanging information and communicating with others, including phones, computers, the internet, tablets, social network sites, and apps. In this 2021 chapter, emerging technologies are recently developed technologies in early public dissemination, with less known about their use and effects. Examples include robots, virtual reality, voice assistants, smart homes, and telehealth applications.

cards.title: How does the life course perspective explain older adults' technology use?
cards.answer_30s: The life course perspective connects ICT trajectories with historical context, the timing of technological developments, life stage, and linked lives. Many Baby Boomers encountered technologies during adulthood and employment, while earlier cohorts had less workplace exposure. Present age-group differences therefore reflect different technological histories and social support as well as possible aging processes. They should not be explained by aging alone.

cards.title: Why distinguish age from cohort?
cards.answer_30s: Age is time since birth; a cohort shares major experiences within a similar historical period. Older adults include birth cohorts who were at different life stages when technologies spread and who had different workplace exposure. Cross-sectional data cannot separate age from cohort effects. An age-group difference at one time therefore cannot simply be treated as a change that occurs within individuals as they grow older.

cards.title: What shows that older adults are not one uniform technology-user group?
cards.answer_30s: In the cited 2016 data, internet use was 60% at ages 75 to 79 and 44% at 80 or older; smartphone ownership was 31% and 17%, respectively. Interviews with 41 Toronto older adults also identified six types: Non-Users, Reluctants, Apprehensives, Basic Users, Go-Getters, and Savvy Users. Those subtype proportions describe that small interview sample, rather than national US prevalence.

cards.title: Why separate access, skills, use, and benefits?
cards.answer_30s: Being online matters, but the chapter stresses that access alone is insufficient to obtain benefits. People also need skills to find information and use relevant functions. Even within older age groups, internet access, broadband, device ownership, and functional uses differ. Access rates therefore should not be substituted for measures of proficiency, meaningful use, or outcomes.

cards.title: How does cumulative disadvantage extend the digital-divide explanation?
cards.answer_30s: Early computer and internet access can create later opportunities for education, job seeking, advanced skills, information, and social connections. Limited access and proficiency linked to income, education, or rural location can make those advantages harder to accumulate. Small initial differences may therefore widen across the life course. Even when two people are both online now, past experience can affect how effectively they activate resources.

cards.title: What are important limitations of existing survey data?
cards.answer_30s: The chapter notes that Pew surveys largely cover community residents able to complete phone or online questionnaires. People in care facilities, poorer health, or social isolation may be missed, potentially inflating usage estimates. Other large panels offer richer health and longitudinal covariates but coarse technology measures. Self-reports have recall errors, while device logs also face installation, privacy, and organizational constraints.

cards.title: Apply social causation and social selection to technology use.
cards.answer_30s: A social-causation account proposes that ICT use changes well-being through connection and information, or through distressing content and displaced face-to-face contact. A social-selection account emphasizes prior depression, loneliness, weak ties, or individual characteristics that influence use and outcomes. Both positive and negative pathways are possible, so a correlation between technology use and loneliness or depression does not establish its causal direction.

cards.title: Through which pathways might psychosocial benefits arise?
cards.answer_30s: Four-wave Health and Retirement Study analyses linked internet or email use with lower depression over time after accounting for prior depression, with social contact suggested as one mechanism. In a three-wave New Zealand study, social ICT use was linked to well-being through lower loneliness and greater engagement; informational and instrumental uses were linked through broader participation. These longitudinal associations help distinguish pathways but do not establish universal causal benefits.

cards.title: How strong is the evidence about physical health?
cards.answer_30s: The chapter reports much less evidence on physical than psychosocial outcomes. In a cross-sectional study of adults aged 80 or older, using more devices and apps was associated with better self-rated health and fewer functional limitations. Social use was unrelated to those outcomes, whereas use to learn information and skills was associated with them. The design cannot separate healthier people using more technology from effects of use itself.

cards.title: What are phubbing and the physical-digital divide?
cards.answer_30s: Phubbing means interacting with a smartphone rather than the people physically present. It may disrupt copresence and leave older adults feeling ignored or disconnected. The chapter calls this gap between ICT-engaged generations and older adults a physical-digital divide. However, poorer relationships might also encourage phubbing or make it more consequential, so longitudinal evidence is needed before assuming a single causal direction.

cards.title: Why can technology maintenance become another digital divide?
cards.answer_30s: Continued use requires connection costs, repairs, updates, passwords, and privacy or security management. People with low incomes may lack repair or connection resources, and older adults often depend on the availability of family or other social ties for help. Assistance can solve problems and create social connection, but initial device provision does not guarantee sustained use when maintenance demands arise.

cards.title: Why does the Internet of Things not automatically enable aging in place?
cards.answer_30s: Connected sensors, cameras, and wearables can monitor movement, sleep, falls, or health indicators and alert caregivers to changes. Their contribution to independent living nevertheless depends on adaptable housing, accessibility, affordability, high-speed internet, and maintenance skills. Privacy and security also matter because connected devices may collect data without users' awareness. Technical capability alone therefore does not guarantee successful aging in place.

cards.title: Explain the telehealth evidence and barriers in the chapter's context.
cards.answer_30s: The 2021 chapter cites evidence for remote chronic-condition monitoring, counseling and communication for chronic conditions, and behavioral-health psychotherapy. It also warns that technical assistance may add to family caregiving demands, while less-skilled adults aging alone may lack support. Its policy discussion reports US state differences in access requirements, reimbursable services, and eligible providers at that time; it should not be treated as a current policy guide.

cards.title: What research and policy priorities does the author propose?
cards.answer_30s: The author calls for research on caregiving, monitoring, cumulative advantage and disadvantage, specific forms of use, and life course change. Tailored training should be accompanied by support for repairs, updates, passwords, and interface changes so people can continue using technology. Better collaboration between researchers and technology companies is also proposed. These priorities acknowledge that technological potential does not automatically translate into improved quality of life for every group.

reading_response.title: Practice Answering: How Did You Read This Chapter?
reading_response.instructions: Connect the central claim, a new perspective, specific evidence, and its limits in your own words. Treat family or policy applications as inferences and keep historical evidence distinct from current conditions.

cards.title: A 30-second overall response
cards.answer_30s: I read this chapter as expanding the technology question beyond device provision to cumulative inequalities and continued use across the life course. Tailored training matters, but breakdowns, updates, passwords, and interface changes may interrupt use when help is unavailable. For me, the central point was that maintenance and social support stand between a technology's potential and the benefits someone actually gains.

cards.title: What was most surprising to you?
cards.answer_30s: I was struck by the cumulative-disadvantage account of the digital divide. Early access can open later opportunities for jobs, education, skills, information, and social ties, with advantages building on one another. It helped me understand why two people who are both connected today may still differ greatly in their ability to use digital resources because of their earlier experiences.

cards.title: How did your previous view change?
cards.answer_30s: I had thought that family help largely solved an access problem. The chapter describes older adults relying on the availability of social ties when devices fail or updates cause difficulties. That help can also become an opportunity for connection. I now see technology support as an ongoing matter of relationships, continuity, and resources, rather than a one-time installation task.

cards.title: Why did you focus on pathways rather than a general technology effect?
cards.answer_30s: I found it more useful to ask which use connects to which outcome than to conclude that the internet is simply good for older adults. HRS analyses linked use with lower later depression, while the New Zealand study distinguished social pathways through loneliness and engagement from informational or instrumental pathways through broader participation. These observational findings encouraged me to examine mechanisms while keeping causal uncertainty in view.

cards.title: What evidence limitation stood out to you?
cards.answer_30s: Technology-use statistics may miss some of the most vulnerable older adults. Samples limited to community residents who can complete phone or online surveys can exclude care-facility residents and people in poorer health or isolation, making use appear more widespread. Self-reports also have recall errors, but logs are not a complete solution because installing and collecting them raises skill, privacy, and organizational challenges.

cards.title: How would you connect the chapter to families or policy?
cards.answer_30s: My inference is that telehealth support should address user skills and family workload alongside service availability. The chapter suggests that helping with technology can add to caregivers' responsibilities, while less-skilled people aging alone may lack help. Its 2021 discussion also describes inconsistent US state policies. I would treat coordinated support as a policy implication to evaluate, rather than assume access rules or effectiveness are identical across people and settings.
